name: Science for Every Student
title: Science for Every Student
answer: AI can help science teachers adapt the same investigation for students with different reading levels, languages, and needs, by simplifying procedures, translating them, reading them aloud, and building vocabulary and support tools. The point is full participation in real science work, not a watered down version of it. Every adapted material still needs a teacher's review before the lab.

sections.body: Science classes bring together students who read at different levels, speak different languages, and have different needs, and a single set of materials can leave some of them shut out of the investigation. AI gives the teacher a way to prepare several versions of the same materials so that everyone can take part in the same lab. A procedure can be broken into simpler steps with pictures, put into a student's home language, or read aloud with a tool such as Microsoft Immersive Reader. The investigation itself does not change, only the barriers around it come down. This solves the problem of students being present in science class but unable to do the science.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a science lab, a teacher can use AI to rewrite a lab procedure into simpler steps with pictures, translate it into a student's home language, or have it read aloud with a tool such as Microsoft Immersive Reader. Before a lab, the teacher can generate a short vocabulary list with pictures and simple definitions for terms such as variable, hypothesis, and evidence, which English learners use during the lab and when writing up results, and which also helps native English speakers because science vocabulary is hard in any language. For students with disabilities, adjustments may include recording observations by voice instead of writing for a student with a fine motor disability, or a step by step checklist generated for the lab for a student who struggles with organization. The individualized education program team and the science teacher decide together which supports fit each student. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so these practices apply across the science classes described.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, and it does not carry an evidence label. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what teachers can do with AI tools and how those materials are used in a lab. The only named tool is Microsoft Immersive Reader, mentioned as an example of read aloud support, not as a research result. The claims about English learners, students with disabilities, and native English speakers are presented as practical reasoning about classroom needs.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Every adapted material needs a teacher's check before it is used. Simplified procedures can drop a safety step, and translations can garble a technical term, so a quick review before the lab protects students and keeps the science accurate. The individualized education program team and the science teacher, not the AI, decide which supports fit each student. The goal stays full participation in the real work of science, not a simpler version of it, and the time saved matters only if the result is right.
